checklist.evidence: Checked the CSS custom property behavior, the DTCG 2025.10 stable release (October 2025, Community Group spec, not a W3C Standard), the WCAG 4.5:1 contrast ratio and the invalid-at-computed-value-time behavior. All are correct.
The opening paragraph is hype ('AMAZING', 'absolutely must adopt them today!', 'incredible'). This breaks the 'confident but not hype' tone rule and the brief's must_avoid of generic AI-style claims.

Covers why tokens help small teams, when to adopt them, a CSS variables and React example, common mistakes and trade-offs, and delivers the original angle. References are present and the length is within range.

Every verifiable claim (CSS custom property behavior, DTCG release, WCAG ratio, computed-value-time invalidity) checks out. The only unsupported statement is the 'exciting future' hype, which is a tone issue (i1).

Audience inferred as community (front-end leads, peer engineers). The adoption heuristics, code and trade-offs suit them. Some basics are explained, which is acceptable at intermediate level. The hype opener is the only mismatch (i1).
The descriptive title matches the intro's stated promise: why small teams benefit and when tokens pay off.
The forty-file scenario gives a usable opening and the conclusion calls back to it. The hype lines at the very start damage the skim impression.
It calls back to the forty-file search and ends on 'a one-line edit'. The middle sentence is a recap list of body advice.
Sentences are clean and short, with no run-ons or comma splices. The only stray capital is 'AMAZING' (i1).
The CSS and TSX samples are valid, and the React Card uses var() correctly. The prose matches the code. Not executed, but reviewed by eye.
No flagged-list words and no em dashes. The first lines ('AMAZING', 'exciting future', 'going to be incredible!') read as machine hype that nobody would say aloud.
The FAQ has five genuine next questions in sentence case, the headings are descriptive, and the claim sits near the top. No TLDR, which a roughly 1000-word post does not require.
The reference page is MDN 'Using CSS custom properties'. The post adds an adoption heuristic, a cost comparison, naming-by-purpose guidance and a build-step trigger, none of which MDN covers.

Quotable insight: 'The repeat count and the planned changes decide the payoff, not the size of the company.' It is reasoned and not fabricated. It is somewhat thin and partly conflicts with another threshold in the draft.
The reader leaves with clear adoption triggers, a starter pattern, five mistakes to avoid and a point at which to move beyond CSS variables.
V1: about 2 instances ('Skipping documentation', 'Ignoring the cost' as headings). V2: about 2 ('nobody on the team has the job of catching it', 'can reasonably wait'). Minor.
V3: the draft is overwhelmingly active. The few passives ('is declared', 'are documented') are acceptable.

issues.anchor: Design tokens are AMAZING, and you absolutely must adopt them today! Stop whatever else you are doing and get on board, because this is the exciting future of front-end work and it is going to be incredible!
issues.description: Hype, exclamation marks and stray capitals open an article briefed as practical and friendly, and they violate the guideline 'confident but not hype'. They also undercut the credible forty-file scenario that follows. Delete these two sentences and open with the scenario, for example: 'You change the brand green, search for the old hex value and find it in forty files.'

issues.anchor: Give each design decision a name, start with color and spacing in CSS variables, add a token when a value repeats and write down what each one is for.
issues.description: The middle of the conclusion recaps the body advice. Keep the callback to the forty-file search and end on one idea, for example that a name for a decision is cheaper than a search for its value. Cut the recap list.

issues.anchor: Check every text and background pair against the WCAG minimum contrast ratio of 4.5:1 for body text.
issues.description: The WCAG 4.5:1 figure is correct but is not in the `claims` front matter and has no inline link, although it is listed in References. The W3C Design Tokens Community Group claim also has no inline link in the body. Add both claims and inline links.

issues.anchor: Add a token when a value appears a second time.
issues.description: This conflicts with the earlier trigger of 'more than a handful of places' and with the 'tokenizing everything' mistake. State one coherent threshold, for example tokenize on the second use for color and spacing, and say why. The post would also gain from a concrete worked example of the cost comparison.

issues.anchor: Small teams hit the same wall, and nobody on the team has the job of catching it.
issues.description: This is mildly defensive and fear-led. Lead with the gain, for example: 'Small teams hit the same wall, and a shared token file gives everyone one place to fix it.' Headings such as 'Ignoring the cost' could be 'Plan for the indirection'.

technical_accuracy.evidence: All checked claims and code are correct. The WCAG, DTCG and CSS behavior statements are accurate and the DTCG spec status is stated precisely.

technical_depth.evidence: The CSS variable mechanics, naming layers and build-step trigger are covered. It does not go deeper into semantic versus primitive token layers, scoping, or runtime cost.

practical_usefulness.evidence: Concrete adoption triggers, a starter file, FAQ migration steps and the flash-of-wrong-theme fix are all usable.

originality.evidence: The 'repeat count and planned changes, not company size' angle answers the brief's misconception. It is thin, and no concrete worked example backs it.

structure_clarity.evidence: The flow runs from concept to implementation, adoption, mistakes and trade-offs. The recap-style conclusion (i2) and the threshold inconsistency (i4) cost some points.

examples_implementation.evidence: The CSS and React examples are correct and short, and they match the prose. There is no example of the migration or the semantic layering.

tradeoffs_limitations.evidence: Covers runtime resolution without a build-time guarantee, typos, the native mobile limit and when to wait.

references_support.evidence: The MDN and W3C references are valid, but the WCAG claim is unlisted in `claims` and no source has an inline link in the body (i3).

seo.evidence: The keyword appears in the title, the description and several headings. The secondary keywords are covered and the FAQ questions are phrased naturally.

audience_fit.evidence: The technical content suits front-end leads. The hype opener is a poor tone match for them (i1).

factual_correctness.evidence: Every material claim was checked and holds: CSS custom property semantics, the DTCG 2025.10 first stable release in October 2025 as a Community Group spec, WCAG 4.5:1 for body text, invalid-at-computed-value-time fallback behavior, and runtime resolution of CSS variables.

claim_checks.claim: CSS custom properties are declared with a -- prefix, read with var(), and cascade and inherit
claim_checks.evidence: This is the documented MDN behavior.

claim_checks.claim: The W3C Design Tokens Community Group published the first stable version (2025.10) of the format in October 2025; it is a Community Group specification, not a W3C Standard
claim_checks.evidence: The DTCG announcement of 28 October 2025 matches, and the spec carries Community Group status.

claim_checks.claim: WCAG minimum contrast ratio of 4.5:1 for body text
claim_checks.evidence: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.3 requires 4.5:1 for normal text. The draft gives no inline citation.

claim_checks.claim: A var() pointing at an undefined property makes the declaration invalid at computed-value time and falls back to the inherited or initial value
claim_checks.evidence: This is the CSS Custom Properties spec behavior.

claim_checks.claim: CSS variables resolve at runtime in the browser and give no build-time guarantee
claim_checks.evidence: Custom properties are computed in the browser, and invalid references do not raise compile errors.

summary: The article is accurate and useful for front-end leads, but the hype opening breaks the required tone and needs deleting. Gate answers: it earns a read by showing small teams exactly when tokens pay off, with a practical CSS variables starter, and if no one read it the misconception that tokens are a large-organization tool would go unchallenged. Scorecard: checks 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12 pass, with minor flags on 3, 4 and 11, check 7 fails, V1 and V2 flag lightly and V3 passes.
